shared_context.title: Fixed-graph cooperation model and payoff definitions

fields.label: assumption
fields.value: A fixed population of N individuals occupies a fixed graph; one unconditional cooperator or defector per vertex. Edges mediate interactions and reproduction. All edges have equal strength; there are no reputation mechanisms or contingent strategies.

value.k: number of neighbours on regular graphs; average number on heterogeneous graphs
value.b: fitness benefit delivered to each recipient by a cooperator
value.c: fitness cost paid for each neighbour by a cooperator
value.rho_C: fixation probability of one randomly placed cooperator in N-1 defectors
value.rho_D: fixation probability of one randomly placed defector in N-1 cooperators
value.q_C_given_C: probability a neighbour of a cooperator is a cooperator
value.q_C_given_D: probability a neighbour of a defector is a cooperator

value.step_1: Choose a random individual to die.

result_groups.title: Death–birth analytical mechanism
result_groups.question: When does death–birth updating favour a mutant strategy, particularly cooperation, on a graph?
result_groups.investigation: Source derivation using pair approximation and diffusion approximation, with the cycle treated by an exact special-case argument.
result_groups.grouping_reason: The threshold, worked illustration, cycle special case, general-game equations, and supporting asymptotic derivations share the death–birth mechanism and substantive fixation question. The separately identified Figure 2 numerical investigation remains its own family.

result_groups.title: Death–birth numerical investigation in Figure 2
result_groups.question: How well does the death–birth cooperation rule match finite-population graph simulations?
result_groups.investigation: Figure 2 simulation study across five graph classes, degrees, and N=100/500.
result_groups.grouping_reason: Degree, graph class, and population-size variations are settings within one simulation study and do not justify family splitting. Analytical predictions are retained as non-closing comparisons.

result_groups.title: Birth–death analytical mechanism
result_groups.question: Can cooperation be favoured under birth–death updating, and what are the general-game fixation conditions?
result_groups.investigation: Birth–death analytical derivation and boundary-payoff explanation.
result_groups.grouping_reason: The reversal of birth/death order changes the generating mechanism. Its general-game equations and cooperation specialisation are one family, separate from the death–birth and imitation mechanisms.

result_groups.title: Imitation analytical mechanism
result_groups.question: When does imitation favour fixation of cooperation or another strategy on a graph?
result_groups.investigation: Imitation transition derivation, general-game criteria, cycle special case, and self-loop interpretation.
result_groups.grouping_reason: All local results arise from imitation, including its self-loop relation to death–birth. A mathematical relation between mechanisms does not merge their distinct families. Supplementary Figure 4 is a separately identified numerical study.

result_groups.question: How well does the imitation threshold match finite-population graph simulations?
result_groups.investigation: Supplementary Figure 4 simulation study at N=100, w=0.01, across five graph classes and multiple degrees.
result_groups.grouping_reason: All displayed graph/degree curves are settings in one imitation simulation investigation. The updating process and separately identified figure distinguish this from Figure 2; the analytical mechanism remains separately grouped.

cross_group_summaries.title: Updating mechanism governs the cooperation threshold
cross_group_summaries.summary: Under the stated weak-selection and large-population assumptions, death–birth permits cooperative fixation above b/c=k, imitation above b/c=k+2, and birth–death disfavors cooperation. On a cycle the thresholds are 2 and 4 for death–birth and imitation. Low connectivity is therefore proposed to help cooperation for the mechanisms that support it. The paper reports theoretical and numerical work, not human or animal experimental outcomes.
